newsitem.title: USA: Key Republican opposes U.S. troops in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Key Republican opposes U.S. troops in Bosnia.

text.p: The chairman of the House of Representatives National Security Committee said on Thursday he would oppose President Bill Clinton's decision to use U.S. ground troops in Bosnia as a "quasi-permanent human buffer."

"After spending the better part of the year evading the question, the Clinton administration appears ready to finally own up to the fact that it was never serious about its commitment to limit U.S. involvement in Bosnia to one year," Representative Floyd Spence, Republican of South Carolina, said.

Spence had opposed U.S. military involvement in Bosnia last year due to the lack of a solid exit plan for the United States, a situation he said has not changed. "The administration still does not appear to have a credible exit plan," he said in a statement.

On Thursday NATO Secretary General Javier Solana said the commitment would be forthcoming. After a meeting with Vice President Al Gore he said the United States was ready to commit as many as 8,000 troops to a new international force of up to 30,000 that would police the peace in Bosnia next year.
Clinton was to discuss Bosnia with his top security advisers at the White House on Thursday night.
But Spence objected that during the time foreign troops had been involved in Bosnia the political situation had not improved, meaning a military force could be needed for many years.

While Spence said he did not believe in just walking away from Bosnia, the United States could play a significant role without committing troops "to serve on the ground as a quasi-permanent buffer between seemingly intractable ethnic and political forces." He did not offer alternatives.
